Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (Centres de Santé de Base, CSB) in Madagascar predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording, including consultations, vaccinations, prenatal care, and dispensing. Monthly activity reports (RMA) are compiled manually at CSB and aggregated/entered into DHIS2 at district level (SDSP), not at point-of-service.Plan Stratégique de Renforcement du Système d'Information Sanitaire 2023-2027 Electronic RMA piloted in 10 districts (e.g., Manjakandriana, Manakara) since 2021, allowing direct DHIS2 entry at some CSB, but limited to aggregate data, not individual patient records; scaling planned but not majority coverage.Plan Stratégique de Renforcement du Système d'Information Sanitaire 2023-2027 CommCare app enables digital community health data entry by volunteers (4,300+ users), integrated to national DHIS2 for reporting to CSB heads, replacing paper treks, but clinic-level patient recording remains paper-based.Management Sciences for Health Key barriers: poor network (58% CSB with 4G), energy shortages, low functionality (CSB1: 37% functional), equipment shortages. National ambitions include DHIS2 scaling, electronic registers, patient management systems by 2027, but rural reality lags—digital for surveillance/aggregates/pilots, paper default at clinics.Plan Stratégique de Renforcement du Système d'Information Sanitaire 2023-2027

revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (Centres de Santé de Base) in Madagascar record patient data - consultations, vaccinations, antenatal care, dispensing - almost entirely on paper registers. Monthly activity reports (RMA) are compiled by hand at the CSB and aggregated into the national DHIS2 platform at district level, rather than entered digitally at the point of care. A 2024 routine data quality assessment of malaria reporting confirms that outpatient registers and other source documents remain the primary tool used by health workers at the facility, with reports subsequently cross-checked against DHIS2 entries made elsewhere in the system. Small-scale digital pilots exist - an electronic RMA trialled in around ten districts allowing some CSB to enter aggregate (not individual patient) data directly into DHIS2, and the CommCare mobile application used by over 4,300 community health volunteers for community-level care and reporting - but these do not extend to routine clinical recordkeeping inside rural clinics. Persistent barriers include unreliable 4G coverage (around 58% of CSB), energy shortages, and equipment shortages, meaning paper remains the default at the point of service despite national ambitions for digital patient records by 2027.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Madagascar, primarily managed by the National Gendarmerie, rely on entirely paper-based recording for criminal cases and complaints. APT guidelines mandate paper custody registers (registres de garde à vue) at all stations, including rural ones, as a core procedural guarantee.APT Guide No evidence found of routine digital case management at point-of-service in rural facilities. Digital efforts are limited to central-level initiatives like a planned UNDP-supported software for judicial file tracking in police technique/scientifique police (2025 tender),UNGM UNDP and laptop donations to gendarmerie for basic admin (2025).MFT Justice sector has LOGIPENAL etc. for courts since 2018, but not extended to rural police recording.E-Governance Report Key barriers: low rural electricity (15%), internet access (~2% rural women), digital literacy gaps, ad hoc training, poor infrastructure, paper archives.Cybersecurity Review; Daily Maverick. National digital ambitions (PRODIGY ID system, e-gov) focus on civil registry/services, not police case dockets; rural point-of-service remains manual with later aggregation if any.

revised_comments: Rural police and gendarmerie stations in Madagascar continue to record criminal cases and complaints entirely on paper. Custody registers (registres de garde à vue), mandated by national guidelines, remain the standard tool at all stations, including rural brigades. Digitalisation efforts to date are concentrated in the courts rather than the police: the Ministry of Justice's Logicivil case-management software, rolled out with USAID/UNDP support to a handful of Tribunaux de Première Instance from 2024, does not extend to police or gendarmerie recordkeeping, and a 2025 UNDP tender for judicial file-tracking software specific to the police technique et scientifique remains at the procurement stage rather than in use. The gendarmerie, which covers around 90% of national territory and the large majority of rural areas, has received basic IT equipment donations but no evidence indicates routine digital case recording at rural stations. Structural barriers - low rural electricity access, minimal internet penetration, and limited digital literacy - continue to constrain any shift away from paper-based dockets.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (municipalities/fokontany) in Madagascar primarily record births using paper forms and maintain manual registers locally, with no centralized national digital repository.SSA POMS The CRVS system is inoperative nationally and functional only in urban areas like Antananarivo, where registers exist but are digitized post-collection; rural facilities lack comparable systems and resources.PMC Study Digital initiatives like the World Bank PRODIGY project plan hybrid analog-digital processes with offline apps for CR offices, as two-thirds lack stable internet, but remain in design/pilot phase (e.g., 2023 Toamasina trial, urban focus).World Bank OIF supports registration drives (65k targeted 2024-25), but no evidence of routine digital use at rural point-of-service. Barriers include connectivity, understaffing, remoteness. National policy aims e-CRVS and biometric ID, but rural reality is predominantly paper-based with low completeness.

revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Madagascar - typically located in communes and fokontany - record births, deaths and marriages on paper registers, with no unified national digital repository. Madagascar's Digital Governance and Identification Management Project (PRODIGY), financed by the World Bank and Global Financing Facility, is running a mass biometric enrolment campaign that had registered over 3.25 million adults by mid-2026, and a May 2026 law now allows birth certificates to be issued en masse through that campaign. This enrolment drive, however, operates as a distinct, campaign-based digital process rather than an upgrade to routine registration at the civil registry office itself: ordinary birth registration within Madagascar's roughly 1,700 communes still follows the standard paper-based procedure, and late registration still requires a judicial process. Around two-thirds of civil registry offices lack stable internet access, and a hybrid analogue-digital model (offline-capable e-Fokontany kits) has so far been piloted in only a small number of locations. Rural point-of-service recording therefore remains predominantly paper-based even as national identity infrastructure develops rapidly around it.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Madagascar predominantly rely on paper-based registers for recording attendance, administrative data, and learning outcomes. The national Education Management Information System (EMIS) uses annual school censuses with questionnaires (levels 1-3 for public schools) likely completed manually at facilities and aggregated centrally via a data warehouse and SDMX standards, as per recent PAPESI project enhancements focusing on ministry-level capacity and infrastructure—not point-of-service digital tools in rural areas UNESCO IIEP; UNESCO EMIS. Isolated donor-funded pilots provide solar-powered tablets for teaching content in ~15-20 rural schools (e.g., Solar United Madagascar, SEED projects 2024-2026), but these target learning delivery, not administrative data recording, and represent a tiny fraction of facilities SEED Madagascar. No evidence of majority rural digital adoption. Key barriers: electricity/internet deficits (only 8% rural communes connected pre-2010) World Bank ICT, untrained teachers (many FRAM parent-hired), poor infrastructure. National EMIS ambitions contrast sharply with rural paper-dominant reality.

revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Madagascar record attendance, examination registration and pupil performance almost entirely on paper. A 2025 qualitative study of the CISCO of Toliara I - a rural school district - found that digital reforms remain largely at the planning stage, with attendance monitoring, examination registration, recordkeeping and school-family communication still paper-based and fragmented, and teachers and administrators describing digital identification cards, centralised servers and automated parental alerts as aspirations rather than current practice. Nationally, the Ministry of National Education's annual school censuses (feeding the Education Management Information System) are also completed manually and take around six months to compile, though a World Bank-financed programme is now equipping school principals with tablets and smartphones for real-time reporting as data systems are digitised. Isolated donor-funded pilots (solar-powered tablets for teaching content in a small number of schools) target learning delivery rather than administrative recordkeeping. Persistent barriers - unreliable electricity and internet access, limited digital equipment, and gaps in digital skills among teachers and school principals - mean paper remains the default recording method in rural schools.
